newsitem.title: JAPAN: Uncertainty over future hits Sega, Bandai shares.
newsitem.headline: Uncertainty over future hits Sega, Bandai shares.

text.p: Investors reacted coolly on Friday to the planned union of video-game giant Sega and toy maker Bandai Corp, shunning shares in both companies.

Although billed as a formidable alliance combining characters such as Bandai's Power Rangers and Sega's Street Fighters, stock market pundits were worried the combined company would have a fight on its hands in a tough market.

Brokers said uncertainties over how Sega-Bandai will fare against video-game competitors and glum profits forecasts for both firms in the business year ending on March 31 watered down incentives to buy, brokers said.
"There is potential, of course, but until we see what sort of business they are going to do together, we don't want to invest," a broker at a middle-sized brokerage said.
Based on the merger ratio, Bandai Co Ltd.shares would normally have been expected to rise and shares in Sega Enterprises Ltd, as the dominant partner, would slip.
But the toy manufacturer's shares finished 140 yen lower at 2,420 yen. This was partly because of a steep decline of Sega shares, which slipped by 340 yen to close at 3,320.

For each of the outstanding 46,482,000 Bandai shares, shareholders will get 0.76 Sega share. Based on the closing price for Friday, each Bandai share would be worth 2,523 yen, compared with Bandai's market close at 2,420 yen, a modest premium of four percent over the market value.

On the levels the day before, when the deal was announced, the premium was eight percent and the deal was valued at 129 billion yen ($1.08 billion). The deal was unveiled after the stock market closed on Thursday.
In the wake of the betrothal, due to be consummated in October, Bandai shares climbed into line with the merger ratio, but started slipping soon afterwards.
Brokers said profit-taking started pushing down the shares in the wake of a sharp rise of 200 yen posted by Bandai shares the previous day.

The Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) said it was making routine checks on the price movement and would notify the securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), if there were suspicions of insider trading or other illegal transactions. But it added that the bourse does not disclose its findings or whether the SESC has been notified.
"We cannot comment on Bandai or Sega," a spokesman said.
As the Friday session progressed, some market participants began to feel the shares were not such a good buy, for the time being at least, brokers said.
"Sega was lagging behind its competitors before the merger and its business outlook is not very bright," said Yutaka Sugiyama, analyst at UBS Securities Ltd.

Last December, plagued by excess stocks of its 16-bit games and by losses at its U.S. unit, Sega chopped its forecast for group net profits in the fiscal year to March 1997 almost in half, to 5.3 billion yen ($44.5 million).
Earlier this month, Bandai forecast a net loss of nine billion yen ($75.6 million) down from a previous outlook of a 10.50 billion yen ($88.2 million) profit.

"If the prices whither away, some shareholders may object to the merger, making it difficult for Sega and Bandai to carry on with their plans," an analyst at a foreign securities house said. "They should do something soon, there isn't very much time until the merger takes place on October 1."
